name: Ćevapi
description: Small grilled rolls of minced meat; Serbian ćevapčići are made of beef, lamb, pork or a mixture. They are a national dish of Serbia, and migrants from southern Serbia brought the Leskovac grill dishes, ćevapi among them, to Belgrade, where they became a widely sold prepared food.
how_to_eat: Eat five to ten pieces on a plate or stuffed into lepinja flatbread with chopped onion, kajmak and ajvar.
how_to_order: Order by the number of pieces, usually five to ten, at a grill shop (ćevabdžinica).

name: Karađorđe's schnitzel
description: A rolled veal, pork or chicken steak stuffed with kajmak, breaded and fried. It was created in 1956 or 1957 by chef Mića Stojanović at a restaurant in Belgrade's Košutnjak as an improvisation on chicken Kiev, and is named after the Serbian revolutionary Karađorđe.
how_to_eat: It comes with tartar sauce and a slice of lemon, sometimes with fries or steamed vegetables.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Karađorđeva šnicla' in a restaurant.

name: Pasulj (bean stew)
description: A thick stew or soup of white or other beans cooked with smoked meat such as bacon, sausage or ham hock, plus carrots and onions. It is a winter staple, sometimes called Serbian bean soup in English, and Taste Atlas lists it among the most popular Serbian dishes.
how_to_eat: Serve hot or cold with bread and a side of sour cream or ajvar.

name: Sarma
description: Rolls of sour (fermented) cabbage leaves stuffed with ground pork or beef and rice; in spring and summer vine leaves replace the cabbage. It is one of Serbia's national dishes and is the first dish served at celebrations such as slavas; a meatless version is eaten during Lent and on Christmas Eve.

name: Gibanica
description: A Serbian layered pie of filo sheets, usually filled with white cow's cheese, eggs and oil (lard in older recipes), with sheets slightly thicker than ordinary pita; crumpled sheets soaked in the filling give the gužvara version. It is a national dish, eaten for breakfast and at Christmas, Easter and slava, and appears in Vuk Karadžić's 1818 Serbian dictionary.

name: Serbian salad
description: Diced fresh tomatoes, cucumber and onion seasoned with sunflower or olive oil, salt and a hot cayenne-like pepper called feferon. It is a summer side dish served with roast meat, similar to other Balkan salads.
how_to_eat: Eat it as a side with grilled or roast meat.

name: Krofne
description: Airy yeast doughnuts filled with jam, marmalade or chocolate, made with flour, milk, sugar, butter, eggs and rum and dusted with powdered sugar. Taste Atlas lists doughnuts among the most popular Serbian foods, and consumption rises around Carnival.

name: Serbian coffee
description: Domestic (Serbian) coffee is the most commonly drunk non-alcoholic beverage in Serbia, mostly made at home and shared with friends and family. Most Serbians start the day with a cup, and it may be served with slatko, ratluk (Turkish delight) or rakija.
how_to_order: Ask for 'domaća kafa' in a kafana.

name: Srem kulen
description: A flavoured cured sausage of minced pork, regarded as a premium dried-meat product. The Srem (Syrmia) kind has protected designation of origin in Serbia, held by an organisation from Šid, and Sremska Mitrovica hosts a kulen festival (Sremska kulenijada) in June.
how_to_eat: Slice it thin as part of a meze plate with cheese and rakija.

name: Srem sausage
description: A slightly smoked, medium-ground sausage of beef and pork spiced with paprika, black pepper and salt, from the Srem area. 'Sremska domaća kobasica' is a registered Serbian geographical indication, and a Srem sausage festival is held in Šid each February.

name: Fish paprikaš
description: A thick fish stew made only of fish, ground paprika, onion, tomato juice, salt and water, mostly with carp in the Upper Danube area where it originates. It is cooked in a kettle over an open willow-wood fire, shaken rather than stirred, and served with homemade noodles.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot with homemade noodles.

name: Rindflajš
description: A beef brisket slowly simmered in broth with carrots, peppers, parsnip, onion, parsley and cauliflower, served with the vegetables and mashed potatoes under a tomato sauce of flour, tomato juice, paprika and sugar. The name comes from German Rindfleisch ('beef'); it is a traditional Vojvodina dish usually made for Sunday lunch.

name: Bermet
description: A sweet aromatised wine from Sremski Karlovci and the Srem wine area, usually 16-18% alcohol, made from red or white grapes of the Fruška Gora slopes layered with herbs such as wormwood, cinnamon and mustard seed; each family traditionally kept its own recipe. Bermet is a registered Serbian designation of origin.
how_to_eat: Sip it as a dessert wine or aperitif.

name: Šumadija plum brandy
description: Šljivovica, plum rakija, is Serbia's national drink, and Serbian šljivovica was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2021. Šumadijska šljivovica is double-distilled from fermented plum mash grown in Šumadija and aged in sessile-oak barrels, and is protected with a Serbian geographical indication.
how_to_eat: Drink it chilled from a small shot glass (čokanjčić) as an aperitif.

name: Kajmak
description: A thick clotted-cream dairy food made by slowly simmering milk and skimming the cream, often salted and ripened into 'old kajmak' with a texture between butter and cream cheese. Serbian food writers single out the area west of the Great Morava, especially around Čačak, for the best kajmak.
how_to_eat: Eat it with bread (lepinja s kajmakom), on top of pljeskavica, or inside Karađorđe's schnitzel.

name: Proja
description: A cornbread of coarse cornmeal, salt and water (often with oil and baking powder), baked in a greased pan; the richer projara or projanica, a separate dish, adds wheat flour, cheese, eggs or čvarci. It is a national dish that was popular among Serbian soldiers in World War I, and is usually eaten for breakfast.
how_to_eat: Eat it with kajmak, ajvar or sour cream.

name: Podvarak
description: Shredded sauerkraut cooked with onion, paprika and pepper, sometimes bay leaf, garlic and wine, and rich with lard and bacon fat. It is served with roast or fried meat such as pork, turkey or sausages and is seen as a rural mountain comfort dish.
how_to_eat: Eat it alongside roast meat with proja.

name: Slatko
description: A thin preserve of whole fruit (strawberries, sour cherries, skinned plums) or rose petals. By tradition every guest in a Serbian home is welcomed with a spoonful of slatko and a glass of water, a custom historically found in Serbia south of the Sava and Danube.
how_to_eat: Take one spoonful, then a sip of water; use a fresh spoon if offered a second taste.

name: Užice prosciutto
description: Smoked, dried beef or pork ham from the Užice and Zlatibor area; beef and pork Užička pršuta are separately registered Serbian geographical indications. The Zlatibor village of Mačkat is best known for it and holds a prosciutto festival (Pršutijada) in January.
how_to_eat: Eat it thinly sliced as part of a meze plate with cheese and rakija.

name: Komplet lepinja
description: A flatbread cut open like a bowl, spread with ripened kajmak and a beaten egg, baked in a wood-fired oven for about 10 minutes and then doused with hot meat drippings (pretop). It is a local speciality of bakeries and kafanas around Užice and Zlatibor, sometimes with pršuta added.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot for breakfast, using the lid of the bread to scoop.
how_to_order: Ask for 'komplet lepinja' (or 'lepinja sa sve') at a bakery.

name: Valjevo 'tobacco' čvarci
description: Pork cracklings fried slowly until all the fat is extracted, leaving fine fibres that look like chopped tobacco (duvan). They are mostly made in western Serbia around Valjevo, which holds a čvarci festival in October, and Valjevski duvan čvarci are a registered Serbian geographical indication.

name: Zlatar cheese
description: A fatty white cheese made in villages of Nova Varoš municipality on Mount Zlatar, once from mixed cow and sheep milk and today almost only from cow's milk. Since June 2013 it has been protected with a geographical indication at the Serbian Intellectual Property Office.

name: Sjenica cheese
description: White, full-fat brined cheese from the Pešter plateau around Sjenica, made from whole raw cow's milk or sheep's milk. Both Sjenica cow's and sheep's cheese hold Serbian geographical indications.

name: Leskovac pljeskavica
description: A grilled patty of spiced minced meat (usually pork, beef and lamb, sometimes with bread crumbs); the Leskovac version is very spicy, with onion. Leskovac, which holds the Roštiljijada grill festival every September, is synonymous with pljeskavica and ćevapi, and 'Leskovac grill meat for pljeskavica and ćevapčići' has been a registered Serbian designation of origin since 2007.
how_to_eat: Eat it on a plate with onion and kajmak, or in lepinja like a burger.

name: Leskovac homemade ajvar
description: A relish of roasted red peppers. In Belgrade a pepper salad sold as 'Serbian ajvar' replaced Danube caviar when its supply faltered in the 1890s; 'Leskovački domaći ajvar' is a protected Serbian appellation, also registered with WIPO.
how_to_eat: Spread it on bread or eat it with grilled meat.

name: Leskovac mućkalica
description: A stew of meat that has first been grilled, simmered with onion, peppers, tomato, garlic and hot chillies until the vegetables collapse. The name comes from mućkati, 'to shake or mix'; the Leskovac style, usually pork, is the most popular regional version.

name: Urnebes
description: A spread of white cheese, kajmak and hot chilli peppers with salt, sometimes garlic; its name means 'mess'. It is characteristic of Niš and southern Serbia, where chopped peppers are used, and it ranges from mild to very hot.
how_to_eat: Serve it as a side with grilled meat.

name: Niš burek
description: A pastry of layered filo or yeast dough filled with cheese, minced meat or vegetables such as spinach. The modern round burek recipe is said to have been introduced in Niš in 1498 by a Turkish baker from Istanbul, and Niš holds an annual burek-making contest (Buregdžijada).
how_to_eat: Eat it hot with a glass of yogurt.
how_to_order: Order a portion, usually a quarter of a tray, at a bakery (pekara).

name: Pirot kačkavalj
description: A hard yellow cheese from the Pirot area. Pirot cow's-milk kačkavalj ('Pirotski kačkavalj od kravljeg mleka') has been protected as a Serbian geographical indication since 2013, and Pirot holds a cheese and kačkavalj festival in September.
how_to_eat: Eat it with Pirot peglana sausage and rakija.

name: Pirot 'ironed' sausage
description: A flat dry sausage from the Pirot area made without pork, from goat, beef and mutton with plenty of garlic and paprika, with no heat treatment or additives. It is dried in a draught and pressed ('ironed') with a bottle every day, which gives it its name, and it holds a Serbian geographical indication from the Intellectual Property Office.
how_to_eat: Eat it sliced with Pirot kačkavalj and rakija, or with nuts.

name: Belmuž
description: A shepherds' dish of young unsalted sheep and cow cheese melted in a cauldron and stirred with white and corn flour until the fat separates. It comes from the mountains of south-eastern Serbia, is tied to St George's Day (Đurđevdan) customs, is on Serbia's intangible heritage list, and Svrljiški belmuž is protected with a geographical indication.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot, ideally with sour milk (kiselo mleko).
